subject: Full Syllabus
summary: a final mixed full-syllabus warm-up for the Grand Mock: antonyms, interior angles of a polygon, a second-order ODE, Simpson's 1/3 rule, friction on an inclined plane, the middle-third rule, Euler buckling about the weaker axis, rack and pinion, torsional vibration, helical spring stiffness, jet power, conduction from a sphere (Nu = 2), nozzle exit velocity, gravity die casting and the EOQ

questions.text: Select the word that is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to PROLIFIC.
solution: Concept: 'Prolific' means producing a great deal (a prolific inventor, a prolific crop).
Productive, abundant and fertile are all close to it in meaning.
The opposite is barren (producing nothing), option (B).
Exam tip: When three options share one idea, the odd one out is usually the antonym.

questions.text: The sum of the interior angles of a convex polygon is 1800°. The number of sides of the polygon is ______
solution: Concept: A convex polygon with n sides can be split into (n − 2) triangles from one vertex, so the interior angles add up to (n − 2) × 180°.
Check: each exterior angle of a regular 12-gon is 360°/12 = 30°, so each interior angle is 150° and 12 × 150° = 1800°.
Exam tip: The exterior angles of any convex polygon always add up to 360°; this is often the quicker route.

questions.text: The solution of y″ − y = 0 that satisfies y(0) = 2 and y′(0) = 0 is
solution: Concept: The auxiliary equation m² − 1 = 0 gives m = ±1, so y = Aex + Be−x.
y(0) = A + B = 2 and y′(0) = A − B = 0, so A = B = 1 and y = ex + e−x = 2 cosh x, option (D).
2 cos x solves y″ + y = 0 instead, and 2 sinh x has y(0) = 0.
Exam tip: Check the initial conditions on each option directly; it is often faster than solving.

questions.text: The integral of e<sup>x²</sup> from x = 0 to x = 1 is evaluated by Simpson's 1/3 rule with two equal intervals (h = 0.5). The result (round off to three decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Simpson's 1/3 rule: ∫ f dx ≈ (h/3)[f0 + 4f1 + f2] for two intervals.
Exam tip: Simpson's 1/3 rule needs an even number of intervals; with an odd number use the 3/8 rule for the last three.

questions.text: A 50 kg block is pushed up a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal by a force acting parallel to the plane, as shown. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.2. Taking g = 9.81 m/s², the force needed to move the block up the plane at constant speed (in N, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: At constant speed the forces along the plane balance: P = mg sin θ + μ mg cos θ (friction acts down the plane, opposing the motion).
Exam tip: For motion down the plane at constant speed the friction term changes sign: P = mg(sin θ − μ cos θ).

questions.text: A short column of solid rectangular section, b wide and d deep, carries a compressive load whose line of action is shifted along the depth d. For no tensile stress to develop anywhere in the section, the eccentricity e must not exceed
solution: Concept: Direct stress P/A and bending stress Pe/Z combine; the far edge stays free of tension while P/A ≥ Pe/Z, i.e. e ≤ Z/A.
For bending about the axis parallel to b: Z = bd²/6 and A = bd, so Z/A = d/6, option (C).
The load must therefore lie within the 'middle third' of the depth (d/6 on either side of the centroid).
Exam tip: For a solid circular section the core is a circle of diameter d/4 (e ≤ d/8).

questions.text: A steel strut of solid rectangular section 40 mm × 20 mm and length 1 m is pinned at both ends (E = 200 GPa). The Euler buckling load (in kN, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Euler's load for a pin-ended strut is Pcr = π²EI/L², and the strut buckles about the axis with the least moment of inertia.
I<sub>min</sub> = 40 × 20³/12 = 26 667 mm⁴ (the other value, 20 × 40³/12 = 106 667 mm⁴, does not govern).
Exam tip: Using the larger I would give four times the load (210.6 kN), a common trap.

questions.text: A pinion of 18 teeth and module 4 mm meshes with a rack. The distance moved by the rack for one complete revolution of the pinion is about
solution: Concept: The pitch line of the rack rolls without slipping on the pitch circle of the pinion.
Pitch circle diameter d = mz = 4 × 18 = 72 mm. One revolution moves the rack by the pitch circumference πd = π × 72 = 226.2 mm, option (A).
Equivalently, 18 teeth × circular pitch πm (12.57 mm) = 226.2 mm.
Exam tip: 72 mm is the pitch diameter and 113.1 mm is only half a revolution.

questions.text: A disc with a mass moment of inertia of 0.5 kg·m² is fixed to the free end of a vertical steel shaft of 20 mm diameter and 1 m length, whose upper end is fixed (G = 80 GPa). Neglecting the inertia of the shaft, the natural frequency of torsional vibration (in Hz, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: The torsional stiffness of a shaft is kt = GJ/L, and fn = (1/2π)√(kt/I).
Exam tip: This is the rotational twin of √(k/m): replace k by GJ/L and m by I.

questions.text: A close-coiled helical compression spring has a wire diameter of 5 mm, a mean coil diameter of 40 mm and 12 active coils (G = 80 GPa). Its stiffness is about
solution: Concept: For a close-coiled helical spring, k = Gd⁴/(8D³n).
Note the strong dependence: doubling d multiplies k by 16, while doubling D divides it by 8.
Exam tip: Cutting a spring into two halves doubles the stiffness of each half (n is halved).

questions.text: A nozzle delivers a water jet of 50 mm diameter at 30 m/s. Taking the density of water as 1000 kg/m³, the kinetic power of the jet (in kW, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Power of a jet = (mass flow rate) × (kinetic energy per kg) = (ρAV) × V²/2 = ½ρAV³.
Exam tip: Jet power grows with V³, so doubling the jet velocity (same area) multiplies it by eight.

questions.text: A small sphere of diameter D loses heat to an infinite, stagnant fluid by pure conduction only (no fluid motion). The Nusselt number hD/k based on the fluid conductivity is
solution: Concept: Treat the fluid as a spherical shell from r = D/2 to r → ∞. Its conduction resistance is (1/r1 − 1/r2)/(4πk) → 1/(4πk r1).
So Q = 4πk r<sub>1</sub>ΔT. Writing Q = h(4πr<sub>1</sub>²)ΔT gives h = k/r<sub>1</sub> = 2k/D.
Hence Nu = hD/k = 2, option (B). This is the lower limit of every forced- or free-convection correlation for spheres (e.g. Nu = 2 + 0.6Re1/2Pr1/3).
Exam tip: 3.66 and 4.36 are the fully developed laminar values for flow inside a tube (constant wall temperature and constant heat flux).

questions.text: Steam expands adiabatically in a nozzle with an enthalpy drop of 200 kJ/kg. The velocity at the inlet is negligible. The exit velocity of the steam (in m/s, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Steady-flow energy equation for an adiabatic nozzle with no work: h1 + V1²/2 = h2 + V2²/2.
With V<sub>1</sub> ≈ 0: V<sub>2</sub> = √(2Δh) = √(2 × 200 000) m/s (Δh in J/kg).
Exam tip: Remember V = 44.72√Δh with Δh in kJ/kg; forgetting to convert kJ to J gives a value 31.6 times too small.

questions.text: Gravity die casting (permanent-mould casting) differs from sand casting mainly in that
opts: the molten metal is forced into the mould under a high pressure
the mould is broken after each casting to remove it
it is best suited for steels with very high melting points
a reusable metal mould is filled under gravity alone
questions.ans: (D) a reusable metal mould is filled under gravity alone
solution: Concept: In gravity die casting the mould is made of metal (usually cast iron or steel) and is reused for many castings; the metal enters under its own head only.
So the answer is a reusable metal mould filled under gravity, option (D).

Forcing metal in under pressure is pressure die casting; breaking the mould describes sand and investment casting; and the process suits lower-melting alloys such as aluminium, magnesium and copper alloys.
Exam tip: Metal moulds chill the casting, giving finer grains and better finish but needing low-melting alloys.

questions.text: An item has an annual demand of 3600 units, an ordering cost of ₹50 per order and a holding cost of ₹4 per unit per year. The economic order quantity and the number of orders per year are
solution: Concept: EOQ = √(2DCo/Ch), which balances the annual ordering and holding costs.
Number of orders = D/EOQ = 3600/300 = 12 per year, so the answer is 300 units and 12 orders, option (B).
Exam tip: At the EOQ both costs are equal: (3600/300) × 50 = ₹600 = (300/2) × 4.
